title: Full Mock 02: HCLTech Ascend Simulation — Cloud, SQL & Systems
description: Complete 75-item timed simulation (37 Cognitive + 36 Technical MCQ + 2 Coding) crafted exclusively from unseen questions.

aptitudeQuestions.question: What is the highest power of 6 that divides 120! without leaving a remainder?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Since 6 = 2 * 3 and powers of 3 are scarcer than powers of 2 in factorials, apply Legendre's formula for p = 3: floor(120/3) + floor(120/9) + floor(120/27) + floor(120/81) = 40 + 13 + 4 + 1 = 58.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: For composite k = a*b, only compute the exponent of the larger prime factor (3).

aptitudeQuestions.question: A, B, and C can finish a backend migration independently in 12, 15, and 30 days respectively. A and B start working together for 4 days, after which A leaves and C joins B until completion. Out of a total contract payout of Rs. 15,000, what is B's share?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Total work = LCM(12, 15, 30) = 60 units. Daily rates: A=5, B=4, C=2. First 4 days (A+B): 4*(5+4) = 36 units. Remaining = 24 units; B+C rate = 4+2 = 6 units/day -> takes 24/6 = 4 more days. Total days B worked = 4 + 4 = 8 days, completing 8*4 = 32 units. B's wage = (32/60) * 15000 = Rs. 8,000.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: B worked all 8 days at 4 units/day = 32 out of 60 units -> (8/15)*15000 = 8,000.

aptitudeQuestions.question: Express Train A, 180 meters long, travels at 72 km/h. It crosses a railway platform in 25 seconds and crosses Train B (approaching from the opposite direction at 54 km/h) completely in 10 seconds. Find the sum of the lengths of the platform and Train B.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Speed of A = 72 * 5/18 = 20 m/s; Speed of B = 54 * 5/18 = 15 m/s. Platform length = (20 * 25) - 180 = 500 - 180 = 320 m. Relative speed opposite = 20 + 15 = 35 m/s. Length of B = (35 * 10) - 180 = 350 - 180 = 170 m. Combined length = 320 + 170 = 490 m.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Total distance covered in both events minus 2 * len(A) = 500 + 350 - 360 = 490 m.

aptitudeQuestions.question: A cash register holds Rs. 5, Rs. 2, and Rs. 1 coins in the count ratio 3 : 5 : 7, adding up to Rs. 320 in value. How many Rs. 2 coins are in the register?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Let counts be 3k, 5k, 7k. Total value = 5(3k) + 2(5k) + 1(7k) = (15 + 10 + 7)k = 32k = 320 => k = 10. Rs. 2 coins = 5 * 10 = 50.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Value per ratio bundle = 15+10+7 = Rs. 32 -> 10 bundles -> 50 two-rupee coins.

aptitudeQuestions.question: Six years ago, a father's age was five times his son's age. Four years from now, the father's age will be three times his son's age. What is the sum of their present ages?
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Ratio shift across 10 years: 5:1 (diff 4) vs 3:1 (diff 2 -> scale to 6:2, diff 4). Gap 1 unit = 10 yrs => 6 yrs ago ages were 50 & 10 -> present 56 + 16 = 72.

aptitudeQuestions.question: The average monthly salary of 20 developers is Rs. 45,000. When 1 senior architect earning Rs. 95,000 retires and 2 freshers join, the team average drops to Rs. 42,500. What is the average monthly salary of the 2 newly joined freshers?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Initial total = 20 * 45,000 = 9,00,000. After architect leaves: 9,00,000 - 95,000 = 8,05,000 (for 19 people). New headcount = 21; new total = 21 * 42,500 = 8,92,500. Combined salary of 2 freshers = 8,92,500 - 8,05,000 = 87,500 => average = 43,750.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: 2 freshers bring 2*42500 = 85,000 PLUS cover the -2500 drop across 19 existing staff (19*2500 = 47,500) MINUS the 95,000 architect? Wait: 85,000 - (95,000 - 42,500? Use deviation from new avg 42,500: sum_diff = -52,500 from architect? No, 19*(+2500) = +47,500 net shift, so 2 freshers sum = 85,000 - 47,500? Wait: check 19*45000? Architect had 95,000, remaining 19 had 805,000 = 19*42,368.42! Yes: 8,92,500 - 8,05,000 = 87,500 -> 43,750.

aptitudeQuestions.question: A rectangular campus lawn measuring 60 m by 40 m has two perpendicular paved walkways of uniform width 4 m running right through the center parallel to its length and breadth. Find the total area of the paved walkways.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Area = (60 * 4) + (40 * 4) - (4 * 4) = 240 + 160 - 16 = 384 sq m (subtracting the overlapping 4m x 4m central square once).
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Crossroads area = w(L + B - w) = 4(60 + 40 - 4) = 4 * 96 = 384.

How many distinct permutations of the word `ENGINEERING` keep all the vowels together in one contiguous block?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: `ENGINEERING` has 11 letters: 5 vowels (E, E, E, I, I) and 6 consonants (N, N, N, G, G, R). Treating the 5 vowels as 1 super-block gives 7 items with N repeated 3 times and G repeated 2 times: 7!/(3!2!) = 420. Internal permutations of the 5 vowels (3 E's, 2 I's): 5!/(3!2!) = 10. Total = 420 * 10 = 4,200.

aptitudeQuestions.question: A tray contains 12 microchips, of which 4 are defective and 8 are functional. If 3 chips are selected at random without replacement, what is the probability that AT LEAST ONE selected chip is defective?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Complement P(0 defective) = C(8,3) / C(12,3) = 56 / 220 = 14 / 55. Therefore P(at least 1 defective) = 1 - 14/55 = 41/55.

aptitudeQuestions.question: Eight people A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H sit around a circular table facing the center. B sits third to the left of A. D sits directly opposite B. F sits immediately between A and C (so A, F, C occupy three adjacent seats). E is an immediate neighbor of neither B nor C, and sits second to the left of H. Who sits directly opposite G?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Index seats 0..7 clockwise (facing center, so left moves +1 clockwise). Put A=0 -> B=3 (3rd left). Opposite B(3) is D=7. For F to sit immediately between A(0) and C, C must be at 2 (F=1) since seat 7 is already occupied by D. Remaining seats are {4, 5, 6} for E, G, H. E cannot neighbor C(2) or B(3), eliminating 4 -> E is in {5, 6}. Testing E = H + 2: only H=4, E=6 fits unoccupied seats, leaving G=5. Opposite G(5) is seat 1 = F.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Fix A=0, B=3, D=7, forcing C=2 and F=1; then E cannot take seat 4 (next to B) and E = H + 2 uniquely forces H=4, E=6, G=5 -> opposite G(5) is F(1).

aptitudeQuestions.question: If 'X @ Y' means X is the mother of Y; 'X # Y' means X is the husband of Y; 'X $ Y' means X is the sister of Y; and 'X % Y' means X is the son of Y, how is P related to T in the expression `P % Q @ R $ S # T`?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: `P % Q` -> P is Q's son. `Q @ R` -> Q is R's mother (so P and R are siblings, P is male). `R $ S` -> R is S's sister (so P, R, S are siblings). `S # T` -> S is T's husband (so T is S's wife). Thus P is the brother of T's husband = T's brother-in-law.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Chain genders & generations: P(+1 male) child of Q; R,S siblings of P; S marries T => P is T's brother-in-law.

aptitudeQuestions.question: In a single row of campus interviewees facing North, Arjun sits 18th from the left end and Meera sits 15th from the right end. If exactly 4 candidates sit between them and Meera sits somewhere to the left of Arjun, how many candidates are in the row?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Because Meera sits to the left of Arjun while being counted from the right, their spans overlap: Total = (Left rank + Right rank) - (Between + 2) = 18 + 15 - (4 + 2) = 33 - 6 = 27.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Overlap total = L + R - between - 2 = 18 + 15 - 4 - 2 = 27.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Statements: (1) All firewalls are proxies. (2) Some proxies are load-balancers. (3) No load-balancer is stateless.
Conclusions:
I. Some proxies are not stateless.
II. All firewalls being stateless is a possibility.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Since some proxies are load-balancers and no load-balancer is stateless, those shared proxies cannot be stateless (Conclusion I follows). Firewalls sit inside proxies with no direct prohibition against overlapping stateless outside load-balancers, so all firewalls being stateless is a valid possibility (Conclusion II follows).
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Proxies ∩ LBs ∉ Stateless => I true; no constraint links Firewalls & Stateless => II possible.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Is the integer K odd?
Statement I: 3K + 5 is an even integer.
Statement II: K^2 + 3K is divisible by 2.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Statement I: 3K + 5 is even => 3K must be odd (since odd + odd = even) => K MUST be odd (sufficient!). Statement II: K^2 + 3K = K(K + 3). Notice if K is even, K(K+3) is even; if K is odd, K+3 is even so K(K+3) is ALSO even! Thus II holds for every integer K and determines nothing.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: K(K+3) has opposite parity factors, so it is always even for all integers K.

Select the letter cluster related to `MICRO` in the same way `DNRYI` is related to `CLOUD`:
`CLOUD : DNRYI :: MICRO : ?`
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Each letter shifts forward progressively by +1, +2, +3, +4, +5: C(+1)=D, L(+2)=N, O(+3)=R, U(+4)=Y, D(+5)=I. Applying +1, +2, +3, +4, +5 to `MICRO`: M(+1)=N, I(+2)=K, C(+3)=F, R(+4)=V, O(+5)=T => `NKFVT`.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Progressive +1, +2, +3, +4, +5 shift across the 5 letters.

aptitudeQuestions.question: In a campus survey of 150 graduates, 90 know Java, 75 know Python, and 35 know Go. Further, 30 know both Java and Python, 20 know both Python and Go, 25 know both Java and Go, and 10 know all three languages. How many graduates know NONE of these three languages?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: By inclusion-exclusion: |J ∪ P ∪ G| = 90 + 75 + 35 - 30 - 20 - 25 + 10 = 200 - 75 + 10 = 135. Graduates knowing none = 150 - 135 = 15.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Given relationship chain: `P >= Q > R = S <= T < U`.
Evaluate Conclusions:
I. `P > S`
II. `U > R`
Which conclusion(s) definitely hold?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: From `P >= Q > R = S`, strict `>` dominates `>=` and `=`, proving `P > S` (I is true). From `R = S <= T < U`, strict `<` gives `R < U` i.e. `U > R` (II is true).
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: All symbols point cleanly in the same direction for both pairs with at least one strict `>`/`<`.

aptitudeQuestions.question: A solid wooden cube painted blue on all six outer faces is sliced evenly into 64 identical smaller unit cubes. How many of these smaller cubes have EXACTLY TWO faces painted blue?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: 64 = 4^3, so side n = 4. Unit cubes with exactly 2 painted faces lie exclusively along the 12 edges (excluding the 8 corners): 12 * (n - 2) = 12 * (4 - 2) = 24.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Formula for 2-face painted cubes: 12 * (n - 2) where n = cbrt(64) = 4.

aptitudeQuestions.question: An SRE team argues that adding distributed correlation IDs across HTTP headers cut their Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) by half. Which finding would MOST strongly reinforce their claim?
options: Most incidents occurred on Monday mornings during traffic surges.
Teams using the exact same microservice framework without correlation IDs saw zero MTTR improvement over the same six-month window.
The SRE team hired two junior monitoring analysts at the end of the quarter.
HTTP header payloads increased by 48 bytes per request.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: A matched control group lacking the intervention (correlation IDs) showing zero improvement rules out external seasonal or tooling trends.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Look for a controlled comparison isolating the proposed cause.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Statement: Internal telemetry revealed that an exposed staging API endpoint leaked 2,000 test customer emails over the weekend.
Courses of Action:
I. Immediately revoke the staging endpoint's public ingress rule and rotate any shared API credentials.
II. Permanently delete all staging environments and ban developers from testing APIs.
Which action(s) logically follow?
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Course I directly stops the exposure and prevents credential misuse. Course II is an extreme, counterproductive overreaction.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Effective course of action is proportional, practical, and directly mitigates risk.

aptitudeQuestions.passage: Traditional perimeter-based enterprise security operated like a medieval castle: formidable firewalls guarded external gateways, while traffic inside the corporate LAN enjoyed implicit trust. Yet hybrid cloud workloads and lateral-movement malware exposed that model's fragility—once an attacker phished a single employee laptop, internal east-west traffic traversed unencrypted subnets freely. Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) replaces implicit network location trust with continuous per-request verification. Every service-to-service call must present short-lived cryptographic identity (such as SPIFFE/mTLS certificates), undergo fine-grained authorization checks against device posture and least-privilege policies, and remain isolated within micro-segmented network boundaries so a single compromised node cannot pivot across the fleet.
aptitudeQuestions.question: Why did traditional perimeter-based security prove inadequate against modern breaches according to the passage?
options: External firewalls could not inspect HTTPS packets at wire speed.
Implicit trust on the internal network allowed compromised endpoints to move laterally with minimal friction.
Employees refused to connect through corporate VPN gateways.
Cryptographic certificates expired too quickly inside legacy LANs.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: The passage notes that once a single laptop was phished, 'internal east-west traffic traversed unencrypted subnets freely' due to implicit internal trust.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Match 'lateral-movement malware' + 'implicit trust' inside the corporate LAN.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Identify the segment containing a grammatical error:
'Although the refactored pipeline triggered (A) / less memory allocation spikes during peak load, (B) / its cold-start latency remained (C) / noticeably higher than expected. (D)'
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: `spikes` is a plural countable noun, requiring `fewer` instead of `less` ('fewer memory allocation spikes').
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Countable plural noun -> fewer; uncountable mass noun -> less.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Identify the segment containing a grammatical error:
'The client committee interviewed three finalists, (A) / one of who had previously (B) / architected an ultra-low-latency (C) / payments clearing engine in Java. (D)'
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: As the object of the preposition `of`, the objective pronoun `whom` is required: `one of whom`.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: After a preposition (`of`, `to`, `by`), always use `whom`.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Identify the segment containing a grammatical error:
'Despite of the exhaustive load tests (A) / executed prior to Diwali sales, (B) / an unindexed foreign-key column (C) / throttled checkout throughput. (D)'
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: `Despite` never takes `of`. Write either `Despite the exhaustive load tests` or `In spite of the exhaustive load tests`.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Never write 'Despite of' (either 'Despite' or 'In spite of').

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Choose the grammatically accurate replacement for the bracketed text:
The maintenance window is scheduled [between 02:00 UTC to 04:30 UTC] on Sunday morning.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: `between X and Y` is the standard idiom (`from X to Y` is the alternative; mixing `between...to` is ungrammatical).
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: between ... and / from ... to.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Select the most precise replacement for the bracketed portion:
The p99 response time of our new Go gateway is significantly lower [than our legacy monolithic Java proxy].
options: than our legacy monolithic Java proxy
than that of our legacy monolithic Java proxy
compared to our legacy monolithic Java proxy
as that of our legacy monolithic Java proxy
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Apples-to-apples comparison: compare `p99 response time` against `that (the p99 response time) of our legacy monolithic Java proxy`, not directly against the proxy itself.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Singular noun comparison requires `than that of ...`.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Select the grammatically best option:
Experienced backend developers generally prefer deterministic constructor injection _______ opaque field reflection.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: The standard formal prepositional idiom for comparing two noun phrases with `prefer` is `prefer X to Y`.

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Arrange P, Q, R, S, T into a logical paragraph:
P: To eliminate those pauses without sacrificing throughput, modern collectors like ZGC perform object relocation concurrently with application threads.
Q: Stop-the-world garbage collection pauses once plagued latency-sensitive Java trading platforms.
R: Consequently, tail latencies stayed tightly bounded under a millisecond even on multi-terabyte heaps.
S: During a full compaction cycle, every mutator thread froze while the runtime swept and compacted fragmented heap regions.
T: By inserting lightweight load barriers around pointer dereferences, ZGC ensures application threads always observe relocated object addresses safely.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Q introduces the problem ('Stop-the-world pauses'). S details what happened during those pauses ('During a full compaction cycle...'). P introduces the solution ('To eliminate those pauses... ZGC'). T explains the mechanism ('load barriers'), and R concludes with the measured outcome ('Consequently, tail latencies...').
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Q (pauses) -> S (compaction froze threads) -> P (To eliminate those pauses -> ZGC) -> T (mechanism) -> R (outcome).

aptitudeQuestions.question:
Arrange P, Q, R, S, T into a logical paragraph:
P: Edge computing mitigates this bottleneck by executing lightweight inference directly on factory gateways near the sensors.
Q: High-frequency industrial cameras generate gigabytes of raw telemetry per minute on automated assembly lines.
R: Only compact anomaly alerts and aggregated summaries then travel upstream to central cloud data lakes.
S: Streaming every uncompressed video frame across WAN links to a distant cloud region quickly saturates plant bandwidth and inflates round-trip delay.
T: That local filtering slashes backhaul costs while enabling sub-20ms defect rejection on the conveyor belt.
aptitudeQuestions.explanation: Q sets the context (cameras generating huge telemetry). S presents the WAN bottleneck ('this bottleneck' in P refers directly back to S!). P introduces edge computing, R describes what still travels to the cloud ('Only compact anomaly alerts...'), and T concludes with the benefits of 'That local filtering'.
aptitudeQuestions.shortcut: Q (raw data) -> S (WAN bottleneck) -> P ('this bottleneck' -> edge) -> R -> T.

technicalQuestions.question: What is printed by the following Java `PriorityQueue` snippet?
technicalQuestions.explanation: Java's `PriorityQueue` defaults to a natural-order min-heap. `peek()` inspects the minimum (`5`), and repeated `poll()` extracts elements in sorted ascending order: `5 10 20 30`.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Default PriorityQueue = min-heap; poll() yields sorted ascending order.

technicalQuestions.question: What does this Java `StringBuilder` snippet print?
technicalQuestions.explanation: Default `new StringBuilder()` allocates a 16-char buffer (`capacity() == 16`). Appending 17 characters exceeds 16, triggering capacity expansion `newCapacity = (oldCapacity * 2) + 2 = (16 * 2) + 2 = 34`.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: StringBuilder initial capacity = 16; growth formula = (old * 2) + 2.

technicalQuestions.question: What is the output of this Java 8 `Map.merge` snippet?
technicalQuestions.explanation: In `Map.merge`, when the remapping function returns `null`, the key is REMOVED from the map! On the 3rd `"a"`, `2 + 1 == 3` returns `null`, deleting key `"a"` and leaving `{b=1}`.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Returning null from Map.merge() / compute() deletes the entry.

technicalQuestions.question: What does this Java 17 arrow `switch` expression return when `code = 2`?
options: Compilation error: yield missing semicolon or break needed
technicalQuestions.explanation: Arrow labels (`->`) in Java 14+ switch expressions do NOT fall through, and block arms return a value via `yield`. Thus `res` evaluates cleanly to `"TWO_2"`.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Arrow switch cases have no fall-through; blocks inside switch expressions use `yield`.

technicalQuestions.question: What does the following Java 17 `record` snippet output?
technicalQuestions.explanation: The compact constructor assigns `roles = List.copyOf(roles)` before setting the record field, creating a defensive unmodifiable snapshot. Mutating `src` afterward does NOT mutate `u.roles()`, which prints `[DEV]`.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: List.copyOf(src) makes a defensive immutable copy decoupled from src.

technicalQuestions.question: Ten threads each execute `counter++` 1,000 times on `private volatile int counter = 0;` without synchronization. Why is the final value frequently less than 10,000?
options: `volatile` disables CPU L1 caching completely causing lost writes
`volatile` guarantees visibility across threads, NOT atomicity—`counter++` is a compound read-modify-write operation
The JVM silently drops increments from non-daemon threads
technicalQuestions.explanation: `counter++` compiles to read -> increment -> write; two threads can read the same `volatile` value and overwrite each other. Use `AtomicInteger` (CAS) or `synchronized` for compound atomicity.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: volatile = visibility + ordering, NOT atomicity.

technicalQuestions.question: If a developer creates a custom class named `java.lang.String` on the application classpath and tries to load it via the Application ClassLoader, what prevents it from replacing the JDK's `java.lang.String`?
options: The Garbage Collector evicts duplicate class definitions
The Parent Delegation Model forwards loading upward first, so the Bootstrap ClassLoader always loads the core JDK `java.lang.String` (and `java.*` packages are prohibited in user loaders)
JIT inlining strips custom package prefixes
The `final` keyword on `String` stops bytecode compilation
technicalQuestions.explanation: JVM ClassLoaders delegate upward (`Application -> Platform -> Bootstrap`) before attempting local lookup, preventing core JDK classes from being spoofed.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Parent delegation protects core java.* classes via Bootstrap ClassLoader.

technicalQuestions.question: In a Spring Boot `@Service`, public method `outer()` (non-transactional) directly calls `this.inner()`, where `inner()` is annotated with `@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)`. Why does no new database transaction start for `inner()`?
options: Spring AOP uses dynamic proxies; internal `this.inner()` bypasses the proxy wrapper and invokes the raw target object directly
Spring Boot disables transactions on void methods
technicalQuestions.explanation: Spring AOP intercepts only external calls crossing the proxy boundary. Self-invocation (`this.method()`) bypasses the AOP proxy completely.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: AOP proxy self-invocation trap: external bean call required for @Transactional/@Async/@Cacheable.

technicalQuestions.question: Two beans implement `PaymentGateway`: `StripeGateway` (annotated `@Primary`) and `RazorpayGateway` (named `"razorpay"`). A service constructor specifies `@Qualifier("razorpay") PaymentGateway gw`. Which bean does Spring inject?
options: Spring injects a dynamic proxy delegating to both
technicalQuestions.explanation: `@Primary` sets the default candidate when no qualifier is given, whereas an explicit `@Qualifier` always wins over `@Primary`.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: @Qualifier (explicit) > @Primary (default fallback).

technicalQuestions.question: Which `CompletableFuture` method flattens an asynchronous transformation `Function<T, CompletableFuture<U>>` instead of returning a nested `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>`?
technicalQuestions.explanation: `thenApply` behaves like `Stream.map` (synchronous transform), whereas `thenCompose` behaves like `Stream.flatMap`, flattening dependent async futures.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: thenApply = map; thenCompose = flatMap.

technicalQuestions.question: Why does the 'Favor Composition over Inheritance' principle warn against subclassing concrete utility classes like `Properties extends Hashtable` in Java?
options: Inheritance forbids adding new methods in the child class
Inheritance exposes inherited public mutators (`Hashtable.put`) that bypass subclass invariants and tightly couples child classes to parent implementation changes
Composition runs 10x faster at the CPU instruction level
technicalQuestions.explanation: Concrete inheritance leaks base-class methods (like `Hashtable.put(Object, Object)` bypassing `Properties.setProperty(String, String)`) and creates fragile base-class coupling.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Inheritance exposes parent internals/mutators; composition wraps a private dependency cleanly.

technicalQuestions.question: According to the Dependency Inversion Principle (the 'D' in SOLID), how should a high-level `OrderService` interact with a low-level `PostgresOrderRepository`?
options: `OrderService` should instantiate `new PostgresOrderRepository()` directly inside its constructor
Both `OrderService` and `PostgresOrderRepository` should depend on an `OrderRepository` abstraction owned by the domain layer
`OrderService` should execute raw JDBC strings directly to eliminate layers
technicalQuestions.explanation: DIP dictates that high-level policy modules must not depend on concrete low-level details; both should depend on abstractions (interfaces).
technicalQuestions.shortcut: High-level + Low-level -> both depend on Abstractions.

technicalQuestions.question: To make a standard Java class strictly immutable (like `String`), which step is ESSENTIAL when the class holds a mutable field like `java.util.Date birthDate`?
options: Perform defensive copying (`new Date(birthDate.getTime())`) in both the constructor and the getter method
technicalQuestions.explanation: Marking a reference `final` only locks the pointer, NOT the `Date` object's internal `setTime()` state! You must defensively copy on both ingress (constructor) and egress (getter).
technicalQuestions.shortcut: final reference != immutable target object -> defensive copy on constructor + getter.

technicalQuestions.question: When inserting a parent record in JDBC and immediately needing its database-generated auto-increment ID for child inserts, which JDBC API call retrieves it in one round-trip?
options: `ps.executeQuery("SELECT MAX(id) FROM parent")` on a separate unisolated connection
technicalQuestions.explanation: Passing `Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS` when preparing the statement allows `ps.getGeneratedKeys()` to return a `ResultSet` holding the newly generated primary key(s) safely.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS + getGeneratedKeys() avoids race-prone MAX(id) queries.

technicalQuestions.question: In a Spring Boot application using HikariCP connection pooling, what actually happens when your `try-with-resources` block executes `connection.close()`?
options: The underlying TCP socket to the database server is immediately terminated
HikariCP's proxy intercepts `close()`, resets session state, and returns the physical connection back to the pool for reuse
All uncommitted transactions are automatically committed
technicalQuestions.explanation: Pooled `Connection` wrappers override `close()` to return the connection to the pool rather than closing the physical TCP socket.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Pooled connection.close() = return to pool (and must still be called in try-with-resources to avoid leaks!).

technicalQuestions.question: Which SQL expression safely evaluates `revenue / units` without throwing a division-by-zero error when `units = 0`, returning `0` instead?
technicalQuestions.explanation: `NULLIF(units, 0)` turns `0` into `NULL`; `revenue / NULL` evaluates to `NULL` (no exception), and outer `COALESCE(..., 0)` converts that `NULL` to `0`.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: NULLIF(divisor, 0) converts 0 -> NULL before division.

technicalQuestions.question: Why is `UNION ALL` significantly faster than `UNION` on large tables when you already know the two `SELECT` branches are disjoint?
options: `UNION ALL` uses indexes automatically whereas `UNION` disables all indexes
`UNION` performs an expensive global sort or hash pass to deduplicate rows across the combined result, whereas `UNION ALL` streams rows directly
`UNION ALL` runs queries on GPU cores
`UNION` locks the source tables in exclusive mode
technicalQuestions.explanation: `UNION` implies `DISTINCT` across the combined output, forcing a sort/hash deduplication pass; `UNION ALL` simply appends streams.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: UNION = append + deduplicate; UNION ALL = fast raw append.

technicalQuestions.question: Table `Logs` has 5 rows where column `err_msg` has values `('timeout', NULL, '500', NULL, 'timeout')`. What do `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(err_msg)`, and `COUNT(DISTINCT err_msg)` return respectively?
technicalQuestions.explanation: `COUNT(*)` counts all 5 rows; `COUNT(err_msg)` ignores NULLs -> 3; `COUNT(DISTINCT err_msg)` counts distinct non-NULL values (`'timeout'`, `'500'`) -> 2.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row.

technicalQuestions.question: Which statement accurately compares Third Normal Form (3NF) and Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)?
options: Every relation in 3NF is automatically in BCNF.
Every binary (two-attribute) relation is guaranteed to be in BCNF, and while BCNF is always lossless-join achievable, it is not always dependency-preserving (unlike 3NF).
3NF allows partial functional dependencies on composite keys.
technicalQuestions.explanation: BCNF guarantees lossless decomposition but can occasionally break dependency preservation (when overlapping candidate keys exist), whereas 3NF guarantees both lossless-join and dependency preservation. Every 2-attribute relation is trivially in BCNF.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: 3NF: always lossless + dependency-preserving; BCNF: always lossless, not always dependency-preserving.

technicalQuestions.question: What two strict ordering rules does the Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) protocol enforce to guarantee database Atomicity and Durability across power crashes?
options: Index pages must be rebuilt before reading any heap row.
The undo log record must reach disk before dirty data pages are flushed (STEAL), and all redo log records must be forced to disk before a transaction's COMMIT returns (FORCE-log / NO-FORCE data).
Checkpoints must wipe all committed records from the transaction log.
Dirty pages can never leave the buffer pool until a transaction commits.
technicalQuestions.explanation: WAL requires logging before modifying disk pages (so dirty uncommitted pages flushed early can be UNDOne) and flushing commit/redo logs before reporting COMMIT success (so committed changes in RAM can be REDOne after a crash).
technicalQuestions.shortcut: WAL: Log record to stable storage BEFORE dirty page flush & BEFORE commit ACK.

technicalQuestions.question: Why does creating `INDEX idx_dept_sal ON emp(dept_id, salary)` enable an 'Index-Only Scan' for `SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 10;`?
options: Every column referenced in both the `WHERE` and `SELECT` clauses resides inside the index leaf entries, eliminating random heap-table lookups
The optimizer drops the primary key table
technicalQuestions.explanation: When an index contains all columns needed by a query (a covering index), the engine satisfies the query directly from index pages (subject to visibility-map checks in MVCC) without touching table heap pages.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Covering index satisfies WHERE + SELECT directly from index leaves.

technicalQuestions.question: A paging system uses a single-level page table in RAM. TLB lookup takes 20 ns, RAM access takes 100 ns, and the TLB hit ratio is 90%. What is the Effective Access Time (EAT) for a memory read?
technicalQuestions.explanation: On a TLB hit (90%): 20 ns (TLB) + 100 ns (RAM data) = 120 ns. On a TLB miss (10%): 20 ns (TLB) + 100 ns (page table in RAM) + 100 ns (RAM data) = 220 ns. EAT = 0.9*(120) + 0.1*(220) = 108 + 22 = 130 ns.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: EAT = TLB + RAM + (1 - hitRate)*RAM = 20 + 100 + 0.1*100 = 130 ns.

technicalQuestions.question: Low-priority Task L holds mutex M needed by High-priority Task H, while Medium-priority Task M_cpu continuously preempts L and runs indefinitely. What is this pathology called, and how does an RTOS resolve it?
options: Starvation; resolved by switching to FIFO scheduling
Unbounded Priority Inversion; resolved via Priority Inheritance Protocol (temporarily boosting L to H's priority while L holds M)
Convoy Effect; resolved by lowering time quantum
Thrashing; resolved by adding swap space
technicalQuestions.explanation: Medium-priority tasks indirectly starve High-priority Task H because L cannot release the mutex. Priority Inheritance temporarily elevates L's priority to H's so L completes its critical section and releases M.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Medium preempts Low blocking High = Priority Inversion -> fix with Priority Inheritance.

technicalQuestions.question: A 32-bit virtual address space uses 4 KB (`4096`-byte) pages, and each page table entry (PTE) occupies 4 bytes. What is the maximum memory required for a single process's full flat single-level page table?
technicalQuestions.explanation: Page offset = log2(4096) = 12 bits. Remaining VPN bits = 32 - 12 = 20 bits => 2^20 = 1M page table entries. Size = 2^20 * 4 bytes = 4 MB per process.

technicalQuestions.question: What is the primary disadvantage of a pure Many-to-One (user-level threads mapped to a single kernel thread) threading library on a multi-core CPU?
options: Context switching between user threads requires a full kernel trap
A single blocking system call by one user thread blocks the entire process, and threads cannot execute in parallel across multiple CPU cores
User threads cannot share heap memory
technicalQuestions.explanation: Because the OS kernel sees only one kernel-schedulable entity in Many-to-One, any blocking syscall stalls all user threads and multi-core parallelism is impossible.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Many-to-One: fast user switch, but one blocking syscall freezes all & zero multi-core parallelism.

technicalQuestions.question: An IPv4 datagram of total size 4020 bytes (20-byte IP header + 4000-byte payload) must traverse a link with MTU = 1500 bytes. What is the payload size and Fragment Offset (in 8-byte units) of the SECOND fragment?
technicalQuestions.explanation: Max payload per fragment = MTU - 20 = 1480 bytes (already divisible by 8: 1480 / 8 = 185). Fragment 1 carries bytes 0..1479 (1480B, offset=0, MF=1). Fragment 2 carries bytes 1480..2959 (1480B, offset = 1480/8 = 185, MF=1). Fragment 3 carries remaining 1040B (offset=370, MF=0).
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Payload = floor((MTU-20)/8)*8 = 1480; 2nd fragment offset = 1480 / 8 = 185.

technicalQuestions.question: How did TLS 1.3 cut connection setup latency compared to TLS 1.2 while also strengthening security?
options: By switching from TCP to raw ICMP
By dropping legacy RSA key exchange (enforcing ephemeral ECDHE forward secrecy) and sending client key shares in the initial ClientHello for a 1-RTT handshake
By encrypting only HTTP headers and leaving bodies plaintext
technicalQuestions.explanation: TLS 1.3 eliminates RSA static key transport and sends speculative DH key shares right in `ClientHello`, completing full authenticated encrypted setup in 1 round trip (or 0-RTT resumption).
technicalQuestions.shortcut: TLS 1.3 = mandatory forward secrecy + 1-RTT handshake.

technicalQuestions.question: When your laptop queries your ISP's DNS resolver for `api.example.com`, what type of query does your laptop typically send to the ISP resolver vs what the ISP resolver sends to Root/TLD nameservers?
options: Iterative from laptop; Recursive to Root
Recursive from laptop to ISP resolver; Iterative from ISP resolver to Root/TLD/Authoritative servers
technicalQuestions.explanation: Stub resolvers (laptops) send recursive queries asking the local resolver to return the final answer; the resolver then performs iterative referrals down Root -> TLD -> Authoritative nameservers.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Client -> Resolver = Recursive; Resolver -> Root/TLD = Iterative.

technicalQuestions.question: Why does the host performing an active TCP close remain in the `TIME_WAIT` state for `2 * MSL` (Maximum Segment Lifetime) after sending the final ACK?
options: To let the peer flush HTTP cookies to disk
To ensure delayed duplicate packets from the old connection expire in the network and to reliably retransmit the final ACK if it was lost
To wait for DHCP lease renewal
To keep the TLS session key alive permanently
technicalQuestions.explanation: `2*MSL` guarantees: (1) if the final ACK is lost and the passive closer resends `FIN`, the active closer can ACK it; (2) stray old packets vanish before the same 4-tuple port pair is reused.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: TIME_WAIT (2*MSL) prevents stray-packet corruption & handles lost final ACK.

technicalQuestions.question: On an integer array `[-8, -3, -6, -2, -5, -4]` where a non-empty contiguous subarray is required, what must standard Kadane's algorithm return?
technicalQuestions.explanation: Initializing `best = a[0]` and updating `cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]); best = max(best, cur)` yields the single-element subarray `[-2]` = `-2` (a common bug initializes `best = 0` and wrongly returns `0`).
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Non-empty max subarray on all-negatives = largest (least negative) element = -2.

technicalQuestions.question: Combining Union by Rank (or Size) with Path Compression in a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) data structure gives what amortized time complexity per `find`/`union` operation over M operations on N elements?
technicalQuestions.explanation: Tarjan proved that pairing Union by Rank/Size with Path Compression achieves `O(alpha(N))` amortized time per operation.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: DSU with both heuristics = O(alpha(N)) ≈ O(1) practically.

technicalQuestions.question: Which traversal guarantees finding the minimum-hop (fewest-edges) path from source `S` to target `T` in an unweighted graph?
technicalQuestions.explanation: BFS explores vertices strictly in non-decreasing order of edge distance from `S`, so the first time `T` is reached, the path length is minimal.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Unweighted shortest path = BFS; Weighted non-negative = Dijkstra.

technicalQuestions.question: Why did Java's `TreeMap` and `HashMap` (bucket treeification) choose Red-Black trees over strictly balanced AVL trees?
options: AVL trees cannot store duplicate keys whereas Red-Black trees can
Red-Black trees enforce looser height bounds (`<= 2 log2(N+1)`), requiring fewer rotations (at most 2 on insert, 3 on delete) under heavy mutation
Red-Black trees use O(1) memory per node
AVL trees have O(N) search time
technicalQuestions.explanation: AVL trees maintain tighter balance (`~1.44 log N`) yielding slightly faster reads, whereas Red-Black trees require `O(1)` rotations on inserts/deletes (`<= 2` / `<= 3`), making them faster for write-heavy maps.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: AVL = read-heavy (tighter balance); Red-Black = balanced read/write (fewer rotations).

technicalQuestions.question: How does a Canary release strategy differ operationally from a Blue-Green deployment?
options: Blue-Green compiles code on developer laptops while Canary skips testing

Blue-Green switches 100% of production traffic instantaneously between two identical environments; Canary incrementally shifts a small percentage (e.g., 5% -> 25% -> 100%) while monitoring error/latency metrics
Canary requires shutting down the database during rollout
Blue-Green is exclusively for mobile apps
technicalQuestions.explanation: Blue-Green maintains two full environments with instant router cutover (fast rollback), whereas Canary exposes a progressive slice of live traffic to limit blast radius while validating telemetry.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Blue-Green = 0->100% instant cutover; Canary = gradual % ramp.

technicalQuestions.question: Which SDLC process model explicitly incorporates iterative Risk Analysis and prototyping at the start of every cycle, making it well-suited for large, high-risk systems?
technicalQuestions.explanation: Barry Boehm's Spiral Model cycles through Objective setting -> Risk evaluation & prototyping -> Engineering -> Planning.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Risk-driven iterative model = Spiral Model.

technicalQuestions.question: In RESTful HTTP API design, which pair of methods are BOTH defined by RFC 9110 as safe AND idempotent, versus idempotent ONLY (not safe)?
options: POST & PUT are safe; DELETE is not idempotent
GET & HEAD are safe and idempotent; PUT & DELETE are idempotent (assuming target state semantics) but not safe
PATCH & POST are idempotent; GET is not
PUT is safe; GET is non-idempotent
technicalQuestions.explanation: Safe methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) do not mutate server state and are naturally idempotent. `PUT` (replace state) and `DELETE` (ensure absence) mutate state (not safe) yet produce the same final state when repeated (idempotent), whereas `POST` is neither.
technicalQuestions.shortcut: Safe+Idempotent: GET/HEAD; Mutating+Idempotent: PUT/DELETE; Non-idempotent: POST.

codingProblems.title: Trapping Rain Water Between Elevation Bars
codingProblems.statement: Given N non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute the total units of rainwater that can be trapped after raining.
codingProblems.inputFormat:
Line 1: Integer N.
Line 2: N space-separated non-negative integers H[0..N-1].
codingProblems.outputFormat: A single 64-bit integer denoting total trapped rainwater.
constraints: Target complexity: O(N) time, O(1) extra space

starterCode.python:
import sys

data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
n = data[0]
h = data[1:1+n]
# Write your solution here

solutions.python:
import sys

data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
n = data[0]
h = data[1:1+n]
l, r = 0, n - 1
lm = rm = ans = 0
while l < r:
    if h[l] < h[r]:
        lm = max(lm, h[l])
        ans += lm - h[l]
        l += 1
    else:
        rm = max(rm, h[r])
        ans += rm - h[r]
        r -= 1
print(ans)

codingProblems.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space beyond input array.
edgeCases: Strictly increasing or decreasing elevations trap 0 units
